additions.title: Companies Act 2006, section 170: Scope and nature of general duties
additions.quote: The general duties specified in sections 171 to 177 are owed by a director of a company to the company.
additions.why: The statutory basis for the brief's statement that the duty is owed to the company, not to staff (the research log recorded this section as not opened). Limits: says to whom the duty is owed, nothing about assessments or records; the page lists pending changes to Schedule 11A only.

additions.title: Employment Rights Act 1996, section 139: Redundancy
additions.quote: have ceased or diminished or are expected to cease or diminish
additions.why: The legal definition that an AI adoption can trigger: a dismissal is by reason of redundancy where the business's need for employees to do work of a particular kind has diminished or is expected to. An assessment that identifies tasks removed is identifying this. Limits: defines redundancy for dismissal and payment purposes; imposes no duty to assess before adopting technology.

additions.title: BTI 2014 LLC v Sequana SA and others [2022] UKSC 25
additions.publisher: UK Supreme Court, via The National Archives Find Case Law
additions.quote: the promotion of the company's success requires that consideration be given to such matters as the interests of its employees
additions.why: The Supreme Court's reading of section 172: regard to the listed matters is a 'secondary obligation' within the primary duty to promote the company's success, the duty is owed to the company with shareholders as intended beneficiaries, and good faith is generally judged subjectively. Limits: the case concerned creditors' interests and a dividend, not employees; these passages are general remarks on the section.

additions.title: Corporate Governance Code Guidance
additions.quote: Ensuring that board minutes document the discussion that led to the decision, including the issues raised and the reasons for the decision.
additions.why: The regulator's guidance on recording significant decisions, and the source for expecting stakeholder impact to appear in the minute: paragraph 30 asks whether the board can explain how impact on key stakeholders was taken into account. Limits: not mandatory and not part of the Code; written for companies that apply the Code; page shows last updated 3 June 2026.

additions.title: HSE's regulatory approach to artificial intelligence (AI)
additions.locator: Policy statement, 'Assess and manage risks from AI in the workplace'
additions.quote: Health and safety legislation requires a risk assessment to be undertaken for uses of AI which impact on workplace health and safety
additions.why: A regulator stating that an existing statutory assessment already applies to workplace AI: where a use of AI affects health and safety at work, a risk assessment and controls are required. One part of the effect on workers that must be assessed by law. Limits: health and safety only, not jobs, pay or redundancy; a policy statement, with fuller guidance not yet published; Great Britain.

additions.title: Use of artificial intelligence in government (HC 612, Session 2023-24)
additions.locator: Part Three, paragraph 3.8, 'Assessing workforce impacts' (also Summary paragraph 15)
additions.quote: Realising the benefits of large-scale adoption of AI will require changes in the roles of civil servants.
additions.why: An audit finding on this exact point: the NAO lists assessing workforce impacts among the lessons to get right at the outset and found the implications for workforce composition and skills were not yet considered in detail in the government's adoption strategy. Limits: central government; position as at March 2024.

additions.title: Assessment of AI capabilities and the impact on the UK labour market
additions.publisher: Department for Science, Innovation and Technology and AI Security Institute
additions.locator: Evidence judgement 2 (see also judgement 4 on hiring)
additions.quote: Around 70% of UK workers are in occupations containing tasks that AI could potentially perform or enhance, according to IMF estimates.
additions.why: The government's own summary of the evidence a board assessment should start from: high exposure in a service economy, and job postings falling faster in more exposed occupations, with cause not established. Limits: a high-level review of others' studies, not new data; the 70% figure is the IMF's exposure measure, not a forecast of job losses.

additions.title: Canaries in the Coal Mine? Six Facts about the Recent Employment Effects of Artificial Intelligence
additions.publisher: Brynjolfsson, Chandar and Chen; Stanford Digital Economy Lab working paper
additions.locator: Section 1, summary of the six facts (abstract gives the same figure for ages 22-25)
additions.quote: young workers experienced a 16% relative employment decline in the most exposed occupations
additions.why: Large-scale payroll evidence that effects fall unevenly: entry-level workers in the most exposed occupations lost ground while experienced workers did not, and declines were in uses that automate work, not those that augment it. A reason for an assessment to look at who is affected, not only how many. Limits: working paper, not peer reviewed; US data from one payroll provider; the authors caution that other factors may contribute; the paper is revised from time to time at the same address.

additions.title: Good Work Algorithmic Impact Assessment: an approach for worker involvement
additions.publisher: Institute for the Future of Work
additions.quote: help employers and engineers to involve workers and their representatives in the design, development and deployment of algorithmic systems
additions.why: A published UK method for the assessment this criterion asks about, produced with support from the Information Commissioner's Office grants programme: assess effects on access to work, conditions and job quality, with workers involved. Limits: voluntary guidance from a research charity, not a regulator's standard; 2023; the summary page was read, not the full guidance document.

additions.title: OECD AI Principles, Principle 2.4: Building human capacity and preparing for labour market transformation
additions.publisher: Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD.AI)
additions.quote: Governments should take steps, including through social dialogue, to ensure a fair transition for workers as AI is deployed
additions.why: International comparator: the intergovernmental standard the UK adheres to treats transition for workers, through training, support for those displaced and social dialogue, as part of trustworthy AI. Limits: addressed to governments, not companies; non-binding; the page is undated and the year given is that of the revised Recommendation as generally reported, not a date printed on the page.

rejected.title: GPTs are GPTs: An Early Look at the Labor Market Impact Potential of Large Language Models (Eloundou and others, arXiv)
rejected.reason: Read (abstract). An exposure estimate for the US workforce; duplicates what the ILO paper already on the list does. Not added.

rejected.title: The impact of AI on UK jobs and training (Department for Education, November 2023)
rejected.reason: Read. Occupational exposure estimates from 2023, superseded for this purpose by the January 2026 government assessment. Not added.

rejected.title: Employment practices and data protection: monitoring workers (ICO)
rejected.reason: Read. About monitoring and its impact assessment, not job change; already cited under worker consultation. Not added.

rejected.title: Management of Health and Safety at Work Regulations 1999, regulation 3
rejected.reason: Read ('suitable and sufficient assessment'; review on 'significant change'). The HSE statement applying it to AI is the more direct source; not added separately.

rejected.title: OECD Employment Outlook 2023; OECD Recommendation text on legalinstruments.oecd.org
rejected.reason: oecd.org returned HTTP 403 in the first pass; legalinstruments.oecd.org returns a script shell. Not read.

rejected.title: TUC, Artificial Intelligence (Regulation and Employment Rights) Bill
rejected.reason: Recorded as blocked (HTTP 403, browser challenge) in the domain log; not retried, not cited.

rejected.title: EU reporting standards on own workforce (ESRS S1; voluntary SME standard)
rejected.reason: Considered as the reporting-framework item. Not opened: no passage known to bear on assessing job change from AI before adoption, and EUR-Lex has returned empty pages. No reporting framework is offered for this criterion.

brief_check: Nothing read contradicts the approved brief. Companies Act s.170(1) and the Supreme Court in Sequana (paragraph 65) confirm 'the duty is owed to the company, not to staff', which the research log had left for the lead to confirm. The FRC's guidance supports minuting the discussion and reasons. The CIPD figure was not re-read today.
